India largely cleared the $3/day floor b.takeaway: India's lined-up poverty rate in 2024 is 2.29% at $3/day, 14.88% at $4.20 and 78.78% at $8.30.
India largely cleared the $3/day floor b.detail: The three fixed lines use the report's calendar-year distribution estimates. Their different levels describe how much of the population lies between each benchmark. The societal-poverty series instead uses direct survey observations and a line that rises with national median consumption.
India largely cleared the $3/day floor b.whyShowThis: Shows why progress at the extreme line leaves a much larger population below higher living-standard benchmarks.
India largely cleared the $3/day floor b.howToRead: Three lines show the World Bank's annual lined-up headcount estimates from 1990 to 2024 and projections from 2025 to 2030 (dashed) at $3.00, $4.20, and $8.30/day; the fourth line shows India's survey-year Societal Poverty Rate from 1993 to 2023.
India largely cleared the $3/day floor b.mistakeToAvoid: Calendar-year lineup estimates and direct survey years use different timing and methods. A low extreme-poverty rate does not establish nutritional adequacy or economic security.
India largely cleared the $3/day floor b.mobileNote: Compare the three fixed poverty lines at 2024 before following their dashed estimates into later years.

The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand.takeaway: The 2023-reference-year Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand, 6.31 in Chhattisgarh, 3.91 in Kerala and 3.16 in Goa.
The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand.detail: The index averages each person's ratio of $28 to their daily consumption in 2021 PPP dollars. Lower-consumption households receive more weight. The state scores use the atlas's 2023 reference year, tied to HCES 2023-24.
The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand.whyShowThis: Maps differences in the depth of consumption shortfalls without choosing a binary poverty cutoff.
The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand.howToRead: Read the map's printed scale and ranked state values: higher scores indicate larger average shortfall ratios. The map is sequential, not a split around the national average.
The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand.mistakeToAvoid: The score is not $28 divided by a state's mean consumption. It is not a uniform multiplier that would bring every resident to $28.
The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand.mobileNote: Use the ranked values alongside the map to compare states and union territories.

The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating.takeaway: Switching from 2017 PPP to 2021 PPP raised India's 2023-24 extreme poverty rate (+1.55 points, from 1.02% to 2.57%) while lowering its LMIC poverty rate (-3.79 points, from 19.91% to 16.12%).
The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating.detail: The comparison holds the September 2026 release and survey year fixed while changing PPP vintages and their associated poverty lines. In HCES 2023-24, extreme poverty rises from 1.02% to 2.57%, while the lower-middle-income rate falls from 19.91% to 16.12%. The dollar lines belong to different price bases, so their nominal percentage changes are insufficient to explain the Indian rupee thresholds.
The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating.whyShowThis: Separates a change in the statistical yardstick from a change in household living standards.
The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating.howToRead: Each row compares the exact same Indian survey year under the 2017 PPP line (open circle) and the 2021 PPP line (solid dot) in the September 2026 PIP database.
The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare a 2017 PPP poverty rate ($2.15/day) from an older news article with a 2021 PPP poverty rate ($3.00/day) as a change over time; always hold the PPP vintage constant.
The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating.mobileNote: Compare the endpoints within each row. Extreme and lower-middle-income benchmarks move in opposite directions.

Depending on survey adjustment and pover.takeaway: The published estimates vary because both the poverty line and the treatment of survey comparability change.
Depending on survey adjustment and pover.detail: Direct HCES gives 5.25% at $3 and 23.89% at $4.20 in 2022-23. Himanshu, Lanjouw and Schirmer instead impute consumption using earlier surveys and common household characteristics. Their CES-based Tendulkar estimates range from 11.3% to 13.6%; their sector-wide EUS-to-PLFS Rangarajan-equivalent estimate is 25.9%.
Depending on survey adjustment and pover.whyShowThis: Distinguishes disagreement about measuring consumption from disagreement about where to set the poverty line.
Depending on survey adjustment and pover.howToRead: Each bar is a point estimate with its poverty line and survey treatment in the label. These are selected model specifications, not endpoints of one confidence interval.
Depending on survey adjustment and pover.mistakeToAvoid: The full range cannot be attributed to questionnaire changes alone. Compare estimates using the same poverty line, and allow for imputation uncertainty and assumptions.
Depending on survey adjustment and pover.mobileNote: Read each method label before comparing bar lengths. Different lines are answering different poverty questions.

Free public foodgrain and welfare items.takeaway: Including specified free welfare goods raises published average monthly spending by Rs 125 in rural India and Rs 82 in urban India.
Free public foodgrain and welfare items.detail: MoSPI's HCES 2023-24 press note reports rural MPCE of Rs 4,122 without and Rs 4,247 with imputation, a 3.0% boost. Urban MPCE rises from Rs 6,996 to Rs 7,078, or 1.2%. The published averages do not identify the effect on the poorest households.
Free public foodgrain and welfare items.whyShowThis: Makes the valuation of free goods visible while preserving the distinction between a sector average and a distributional effect.
Free public foodgrain and welfare items.howToRead: Each row is a sector; columns show monthly rupees per person without and with the imputed value of specified free welfare goods. Both columns share the same rupee unit.
Free public foodgrain and welfare items.mistakeToAvoid: The percentage boost uses without-imputation spending as its denominator. Free health services and education-fee waivers are not imputed here, and this is not the World Bank's exact harmonised welfare aggregate.
Free public foodgrain and welfare items.mobileNote: Compare the distance between the two spending values within each sector, rather than treating the rural-urban level difference as a transfer effect.

National Accounts spending grew 4.49x si.takeaway: From 1977 to 2023, India's real GDP per capita grew 5.70-fold and National Accounts household consumption grew 4.49-fold, but NSS/HCES survey mean consumption grew only 2.09-fold.
National Accounts spending grew 4.49x si.detail: All three series are indexed to their own 1977 value. By 2023, National Accounts household consumption per person is 4.49 times its baseline, while survey mean consumption is 2.09 times its baseline. The divergence flags differences in coverage, valuation, reporting and survey methods; it does not identify a single cause.
National Accounts spending grew 4.49x si.whyShowThis: Provides an independent consistency check on the growth captured by consumption surveys.
National Accounts spending grew 4.49x si.howToRead: Three lines trace real per-capita growth indexed to 100 in 1977 across the nine Indian survey years in PIP (1977, 1983, 1987, 1993, 2004, 2009, 2011, 2022, and 2023).
National Accounts spending grew 4.49x si.mistakeToAvoid: The chart does not prove that all missing consumption belongs to rich households or that the truth lies midway between the lines. Consumption inequality is different from income or wealth inequality.
National Accounts spending grew 4.49x si.mobileNote: The common starting value is 100. Compare relative growth, not the original currency levels.

Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment.takeaway: Over the twenty-one years from 2003 to 2024, poor Indian households (<$8.30/day) dramatically expanded secondary schooling, yet the share of their working-age adults in employment declined from 60.72% to 58.29%.
Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment.detail: Among workers in households below $8.30 a day, the share without secondary education falls from 86.71% to 56.47%. The employment rate among working-age adults in those households falls from 60.72% to 58.29%, while it rises from 50.25% to 57.58% in non-poor households. The chart does not isolate the roles of age, gender or local job availability.
Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment.whyShowThis: Highlights the central empirical puzzle of Chapter 4 for India: rising schooling in poor families coincided with falling adult employment rates.
Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment.howToRead: Open circles show 2003 levels and solid dots show 2024 levels (in %) for poor (<$8.30/day) and non-poor (>=$8.30/day) households across employment and educational attainment.
Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment.mistakeToAvoid: Poor and non-poor are groups at each date, not the same households followed over time. Employment rates and workers' education shares also have different denominators.
Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment.mobileNote: Compare the top two rows: the Poor employment dot moves left (60.72% to 58.29%), while the Non-poor employment dot moves right (50.25% to 57.58%).

Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 ho.takeaway: Paid employees below $3/day work 44.05 hours a week on average, against 44.95 above the line.
Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 ho.detail: The Box 4.1 comparison uses household poverty status at $3 a person a day. For self-employed and unpaid workers, the corresponding averages are 37.05 and 40.61 hours. These averages describe employed people, not all working-age adults.
Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 ho.whyShowThis: Tests whether differences in hours alone can explain low household consumption.
Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 ho.howToRead: Each row is an employment type. The two endpoints show average weekly hours for workers below and above the $3/day household consumption line.
Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 ho.mistakeToAvoid: Do not combine this $3/day split with the $8.30/day job-structure comparisons as though they describe the same poor workers. Hours do not measure effort, hourly pay or job security.
Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 ho.mobileNote: Read each employment type separately. Both endpoints use hours per week.

World Bank simulation: Closing India's e.takeaway: In the World Bank's Chapter 4 counterfactual (`DataFig4C_123.dta`), raising poor households' adult employment rates and worker earnings to benchmark levels reduces India's $8.30/day poverty rate from 78.78% to 56.61% (-22.17 percentage points).
World Bank simulation: Closing India's e.detail: The supplied processed counterfactual combines employment and worker-earnings changes. At $8.30/day, the headcount falls by 22.17 percentage points and the poverty gap falls from 25.73% to 16.64%. At $3/day the headcount changes from 2.28% to 1.14%; the file does not separately identify India's education and sector contributions to the combined change.
World Bank simulation: Closing India's e.whyShowThis: Shows both the scale and the limits of the report's combined jobs counterfactual.
World Bank simulation: Closing India's e.howToRead: The two columns compare baseline and simulated levels. Headcounts are shares of people; poverty gaps average the shortfall across everyone as a percentage of the relevant poverty line. Percentage-point reductions are described in the text, not plotted as levels.
World Bank simulation: Closing India's e.mistakeToAvoid: This is an accounting counterfactual, not a forecast or a costed programme. It does not establish the causal effect of any particular jobs policy.
World Bank simulation: Closing India's e.mobileNote: Focus on the top row: $8.30/day poverty drops from 78.78% to 56.61%, a 22.17 percentage-point reduction.

Monetary poverty and deprivation measure.takeaway: In HCES 2022-23, the World Bank's multidimensional poverty rate is 17.74%, against 5.25% at the monetary extreme line.
Monetary poverty and deprivation measure.detail: The chart combines different instruments with explicit vintages: HCES 2022-23 for the MPM, HCES 2023-24 for recent monetary lines, NFHS-5 in 2019-21 for child nutrition, and 2022 health-financing observations. Stunting affects 35.5% of children under five; health-cost hardship affects 30.94% of all people in its separate indicator. These are not simultaneous measurements of the same population.
Monetary poverty and deprivation measure.whyShowThis: Shows which forms of deprivation a monetary headcount leaves out.
Monetary poverty and deprivation measure.howToRead: Each bar is a percentage, but the label supplies its population and survey. Child stunting and underweight use children under five; the other measures use people. Source years differ.
Monetary poverty and deprivation measure.mistakeToAvoid: Do not add the bars or infer that a lower monetary rate caused the other outcomes. The MPM excludes health and nutrition; medical hardship is not this article's $3/day poverty measure.
Monetary poverty and deprivation measure.mobileNote: Read the population and vintage beside each bar before comparing its length.

Among Indians below $8.30, consumption a.takeaway: Among people below the $8.30 line in HCES 2023-24, average consumption falls about 34.1% short of the threshold.
Among Indians below $8.30, consumption a.detail: At the $3 and $4.20 lines, the corresponding average shortfalls among poor people are about 13.2% and 15.9%. Each value divides the population-average poverty gap by the headcount share at the same line. The API inputs are rounded, so the displayed ratios are approximate.
Among Indians below $8.30, consumption a.whyShowThis: Distinguishes the depth of poverty from the number of people below a threshold.
Among Indians below $8.30, consumption a.howToRead: Each bar shows average consumption shortfall as a percentage of that poverty line, among people below it. All three rows use the direct 2023-24 survey estimate.
Among Indians below $8.30, consumption a.mistakeToAvoid: The denominator changes with the line: each row describes a different group. This is not the population-average poverty gap or the causal effect of raising a line.
Among Indians below $8.30, consumption a.mobileNote: Read the percentage as the shortfall within the poor group, rather than the share of all Indians who are poor.

A hypothetical 10% real consumption loss.takeaway: Crossing a poverty line can leave little room for a loss of consumption.
A hypothetical 10% real consumption loss.detail: A hypothetical uniform 10% real consumption loss raises the share below $4.20 from 14.9% to 23.2%. At $3 the change is from 2.3% to 4.4%, and at $8.30 from 78.8% to 85.1%. Both endpoints come from the same 2024 population bins.
A hypothetical 10% real consumption loss.whyShowThis: The headcount trend cannot show how many people sit just above a line. This exercise tests the size of that buffer under one explicit assumption.
A hypothetical 10% real consumption loss.howToRead: Open circles mark the 2024 bin estimate; solid dots mark the result after multiplying every bin’s real consumption by 0.9. Each row uses a different poverty line.
A hypothetical 10% real consumption loss.mistakeToAvoid: This is a static sensitivity, not a forecast or a probability of returning to poverty. Bins resolve to about 0.1 percentage point, so the $4.20 baseline is 14.9%, rather than the full national lineup’s 14.88%.
A hypothetical 10% real consumption loss.mobileNote: Read each row as a before-and-after pair under the same hypothetical loss.

The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1%.takeaway: The poorest survey decile gained fastest within the two comparable HCES rounds.
The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1%.detail: Average real consumption increased 13.1% for the poorest tenth and declined 2.9% for the richest surveyed tenth. National mean consumption grew 4.7%. This is a change in decile averages, not a change in each decile’s consumption share.
The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1%.whyShowThis: It shows where measured gains occurred without crossing the older survey-design break.
The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1%.howToRead: Each bar compares average real consumption in a decile between HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24. Bars to the right of zero show growth; a bar to the left shows a decline.
The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1%.mistakeToAvoid: These are repeated cross-sections. The same people need not occupy a decile in both rounds, and the richest surveyed tenth is not a complete account of affluent Indians.
The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1%.mobileNote: Start with the poorest tenth, then compare its growth with the other deciles.

Young children are more likely to live b.takeaway: Young children are more likely to live in low-consumption households than the average resident of their state.
Young children are more likely to live b.detail: SPID records a higher $8.30 poverty share among ages 0-5 than among all ages in all 36 states and union territories. Kerala’s shares are 75.8% and 58.5%; Maharashtra’s are 91.0% and 82.0%. The chart shows 14 selected states.
Young children are more likely to live b.whyShowThis: A state average hides differences in the households where children grow up. This adds an age comparison to the map’s geographical one.
Young children are more likely to live b.howToRead: Open circles show each state’s all-age poverty share; solid dots show the share among ages 0-5. Both use SPID’s direct HCES 2023-24 estimates and the same $8.30 line.
Young children are more likely to live b.mistakeToAvoid: All ages includes the children, so these are nested groups. Household per-capita consumption does not reveal what children receive within the home. These survey estimates differ from the GSAP calendar lineup used for the map.
Young children are more likely to live b.mobileNote: Compare the two dots within a state; do not read them as mutually exclusive populations.

India has lower $3 poverty than Banglade.takeaway: India’s low extreme-poverty share does not imply a similar position at the higher benchmark.
India has lower $3 poverty than Banglade.detail: At $8.30 a day, India’s 2024 headcount is 78.8%, against 68.5% in Bangladesh, 68.1% in Indonesia, 18.2% in Viet Nam and 87.2% in Pakistan. India has a lower $3 share than Bangladesh, Indonesia and Pakistan.
India has lower $3 poverty than Banglade.whyShowThis: Common thresholds reveal where India’s progress compares well and where wider consumption shortfalls remain.
India has lower $3 poverty than Banglade.howToRead: Compare countries within the same poverty-line column. All values are percentages of each country’s population, in 2021 PPP prices for calendar year 2024.
India has lower $3 poverty than Banglade.mistakeToAvoid: These countries are selected Asian comparators, not an exhaustive ranking or one income group. Indonesia is marked actual; the other countries are projections or lineup estimates rather than surveys all conducted in the same year.
India has lower $3 poverty than Banglade.mobileNote: Use the three repeated line labels to compare the same threshold across countries.
